overview:
Kevala‑jñāna (Kevalajnana) is the Jain term for “absolute knowledge” or “omniscience,” regarded across Jain traditions as the highest possible cognitive state attainable by an embodied soul. It is defined as the complete, direct, and unobstructed knowledge of all substances (dravya), their modes (paryāya), and their infinite temporal modifications (pariṇāma). Jain epistemology classifies Kevala‑jñāna as the fourth and final stage of jñāna, surpassing mati (sensory‑based cognition), śruta (scriptural cognition), and avadhi/manahparyāya (clairvoyant and telepathic cognition). In classical doctrine, Kevala‑jñāna arises only when all ghātiyā karmas—those that obscure knowledge, perception, energy, and right conduct—are completely destroyed.

The attainment of Kevala‑jñāna marks the soul’s entry into the 13th guṇasthāna (stage of spiritual development), known as sayoga‑kevalin. Although the kevalin still possesses minimal bodily activity, their knowledge is perfect, infinite, and non‑sequential. Jain thinkers emphasize that Kevala‑jñāna is not a mystical fusion with the universe but the soul’s own inherent capacity, revealed once karmic veils are removed. The kevalin perceives all substances simultaneously without reliance on sense organs or mental constructs.

In Digambara tradition, the kevalin is described as having no need for food and emitting a divya‑dhvani (divine sound) that becomes the basis for scripture. Śvetāmbara traditions describe the kevalin as still engaging in minimal bodily functions and teaching through ordinary speech, though divya‑dhvani remains a shared concept. Both traditions agree that Kevala‑jñāna is attained by the tīrthaṅkaras and certain other liberated teachers before final liberation (mokṣa) at the 14th guṇasthāna.

Modern scholarship highlights the philosophical sophistication of Kevala‑jñāna as a theory of omniscience grounded in Jain metaphysics of multiplicity (anekāntavāda). It is not merely infinite information but perfect apprehension of reality’s complexity, including all standpoints (naya) and all conditional truths (syādvāda).

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.translation: Kevala‑knowledge arises when the knowledge‑obscuring and other (ghātiyā) karmas are destroyed.
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.1–10.2 provides the canonical definition of Kevala‑jñāna accepted across Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions. Commentaries differ on physiological descriptions of the kevalin but agree on the karmic mechanism.

primary_sources.title: Samavāyāṅga Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Śvetāmbara canonical text
primary_sources.translation: The knowledge of the kevalin is complete.
primary_sources.notes: This text emphasizes the totality and non‑fragmented nature of Kevala‑jñāna. It is part of the Śvetāmbara canon and often cited in discussions of omniscience.

primary_sources.title: Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama
primary_sources.author: Kundakunda (attributed) and later Digambara redactors
primary_sources.translation: The knowledge of the kevalin is without doubt.
primary_sources.notes: A foundational Digambara scripture describing the kevalin’s cognition as free from uncertainty and obstruction. The text is central to Digambara doctrinal formulations of omniscience.

misconceptions.myth: Kevala‑jñāna is a supernatural power granted by divine intervention.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine states that Kevala‑jñāna is an inherent capacity of every soul, revealed only when specific karmas are destroyed. No external deity bestows it.

misconceptions.myth: A kevalin knows the future because they control events.
misconceptions.reality: Kevala‑jñāna includes knowledge of all modes of substances across time, but this does not imply causal control. The kevalin perceives reality; they do not manipulate it.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain traditions describe the kevalin identically.
misconceptions.reality: Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions agree on the nature of omniscience but differ on physiological details, such as whether the kevalin eats or how teachings are delivered.
